questions.question: What do the numbers on the ends of a runway indicate?
questions.correct_answer: The magnetic heading of the runway rounded to the nearest 10 degrees, divided by 10
distractors: The length of the runway in hundreds of feet
The elevation of the runway in feet MSL
The runway's assigned traffic pattern number
questions.explanation: Runway numbers represent the magnetic heading divided by 10 and rounded. Runway 27 has a magnetic heading of approximately 270 degrees.

reference.text:
Runway designation marking
Runway numbers and letters are determined from the approach direction. The runway number is the whole number nearest one-tenth the magnetic azimuth of the centerline of the runway, measured clockwise from the magnetic north. In the case where there are parallel runways, the letters differentiate between left (L), right (R), or center (C). [Figure 14-16] For example, if there are two parallel runways, they would show the designation number and then either L or R beneath it.
For three parallel runways, the designation number would be presented with L, C, or R beneath it.

questions.question: Unless otherwise indicated, what is the standard direction of traffic pattern turns at an airport?
questions.explanation: Standard traffic patterns use left turns unless the airport has designated right traffic for specific runways, as indicated in the Chart Supplement or by visual indicators.

reference.text: Nontowered airport traffic patterns are always entered at pattern altitude. How you enter the pattern depends upon the direction of arrival. The preferred method for entering from the downwind side of the pattern is to approach the pattern on a course 45 degrees to the downwind leg and join the pattern at midfield. An alternate method is to enter on a midfield crosswind at pattern altitude, carefully scan for traffic, announce your intentions, and then turn downwind. [Figure 14-3] This technique should not be used if the pattern is busy. Always remember to give way to aircraft on the preferred 45° entry and to aircraft already established on downwind. When well clear of the pattern—approximately 2 miles–scan carefully for traffic, descend to pattern altitude, then turn right to enter at 45° to the downwind leg at midfield. [Figure 14-2]

questions.question: What color are the runway edge lights that mark the last 2,000 feet of runway available for landing?
questions.explanation: Runway edge lights are white, but the last 2,000 feet (or last half of the runway if less than 4,000 feet) have yellow caution-zone lighting to warn pilots of the approaching runway end.

reference.text: The lights marking the end of the runway are red. In-Runway Lighting Runway centerline lighting system (RCLS)—installed on some precision approach runways to facilitate landing under adverse visibility conditions. They are located along the runway centerline and are spaced at 50-foot intervals. When viewed from the landing threshold, the runway centerline lights are white until the last 3,000 feet of the runway. The white lights begin to alternate with red for the next 2,000 feet. For the remaining 1,000 feet of the runway, all centerline lights are red.

questions.question: What colors does a civilian airport beacon alternate between?
questions.explanation: Civilian airport beacons alternate white and green. Military airport beacons alternate white and green but with dual-peaked white flashes. Heliport beacons are green-yellow-white.

reference.text: The beacon may be an omnidirectional capacitor-discharge device, or it may rotate at a constant speed, that produces the visual effect of flashes at regular intervals. The combination of light colors from an airport beacon indicates the type of airport. [Figure 14-28] Some of the most common beacons are: • Flashing white and green for civilian land airports • Flashing white and yellow for a water airport • Flashing white, yellow, and green for a heliport • Two quick white flashes alternating with a green flash identifying a military airport

questions.question: When using a VASI (Visual Approach Slope Indicator), what does seeing two red lights over two red lights indicate?
questions.correct_answer: The aircraft is below the glide path
distractors: The aircraft is on the glide path
The aircraft is above the glide path
questions.explanation: VASI: Red over Red = below glide path (dangerously low). Red over White = on glide path. White over White = above glide path. Memory: 'Red over red, you're dead.'

reference.text:
The VASI consists of light units arranged in bars. There are 2-bar and 3-bar VASIs. The 2-bar VASI has near and far light bars and the 3-bar VASI has near, middle, and far light bars. Two-bar VASI installations provide one visual glidepath that is normally set at 3°. The 3-bar system provides two glidepaths, the lower glidepath normally set at 3° and the upper glidepath ¼ degree above the lower glidepath.

The basic principle of the VASI is that of color differentiation between red and white. Each light unit projects a beam of light, a white segment in the upper part of the beam and a red segment in the lower part of the beam. The lights are arranged so the pilot sees the combination of lights shown in Figure 14-29 to indicate below, on, or above the glidepath.

questions.question: What is the purpose of NOTAMs (Notices to Air Missions)?
questions.correct_answer: To alert pilots of temporary changes, hazards, or conditions at airports and in the NAS
distractors: To provide permanent changes to instrument approach procedures
questions.explanation: NOTAMs provide time-critical aeronautical information on temporary conditions, such as runway closures, airspace restrictions, hazards, and equipment outages.

reference.text: NOTAMs provide time-critical aeronautical information on temporary conditions, such as runway closures, airspace restrictions, hazards, and equipment outages.

questions.question: What does a solid yellow line paired with a dashed yellow line on a taxiway mean?
questions.correct_answer: Hold short line — do not cross from the solid side without ATC clearance
distractors: ILS critical area boundary that can be freely crossed
questions.explanation: The hold short marking has a solid line on the taxiway side and dashed lines on the runway side. Aircraft must stop before the solid line and not cross without ATC clearance.

reference.text: Runway holding position markings consist of four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, that are painted on the surface and extend across the width of the taxiway to indicate where the aircraft should stop when approaching a runway. These markings are painted across the entire taxiway pavement, are in alignment, and are collocated with the holding position sign as described above.

questions.question: When landing behind a large aircraft on the same runway, where should a pilot plan to touch down?
questions.correct_answer: Beyond the large aircraft's touchdown point
distractors: Before the large aircraft's touchdown point
At the same point as the large aircraft
On the first third of the runway regardless
questions.explanation: Wake turbulence (wingtip vortices) sink and drift. Landing beyond the preceding aircraft's touchdown point helps avoid its wake vortices, which are generated from rotation to touchdown.

reference.text: When landing behind a large aircraft on the same runway, where should a pilot plan to touch down? Beyond the large aircraft's touchdown point. Explanation: Wake turbulence (wingtip vortices) sink and drift. Landing beyond the preceding aircraft's touchdown point helps avoid its wake vortices, which are generated from rotation to touchdown.
